notes.meaning: God gives Ezekiel a prophecy about the seaport city of Tyre during the year Jerusalem fell to Babylon. Recording the exact date shows that God's message was tied to real events in history and carried great importance. God watches how nations treat one another and holds them responsible for their actions.

The wealthy trading city of Tyre celebrated when Jerusalem was shattered and conquered. Tyre saw Jerusalem as a competitor for major trade routes and expected that the city's ruin would bring more business and wealth to its own harbors. It is a grave sin to celebrate the suffering of others just to make a personal gain.

The Lord declares that He stands directly against Tyre and will send many foreign nations to attack her. These invading armies would strike her coasts wave after wave, just like the waters of the sea battering a rocky shore. No amount of commercial wealth or military strength can shield a proud people from God's judgment.

The invading armies will break down Tyre's massive defensive walls and smash her tall watchtowers. God warns that He will scrape away her soil and rubble, leaving the city as a flat, bare rock. This statement is a play on words, since the name Tyre itself means "rock."

The site of Tyre will become so desolate that only local fishermen will go there to spread and dry their wet nets. The city that once grew rich by taking from other nations will instead be stripped and plundered by foreign armies. Human pride and dishonest wealth quickly disappear when God calls a nation to account.

The towns and dependent villages on the nearby mainland will be struck down by the sword of the enemy. When these places fall, the survivors will recognize that the Lord is the one true God over all the earth. God reveals His supreme power when He removes false security and worldly reliance.

The Lord names King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon as the conqueror who will lead this assault from the north. Nebuchadnezzar is called "king of kings" because many subject rulers served under his vast empire, and he marches with a huge army of cavalry and chariots. God directs the rulers of world empires to carry out His sovereign purposes.

Nebuchadnezzar will start by conquering the mainland villages belonging to Tyre before turning on the fortified city. His troops will build dirt siege ramps, wooden assault forts, and protective roofs of shields to storm the walls. Earthly defenses are useless when God brings an end to a nation's pride.

The Babylonian army will pound heavy battering rams against the walls of Tyre until the stone gives way. Soldiers will then use heavy iron weapons to tear down the high defensive towers. Human engineering and tall fortress walls cannot stop the judgment of the Lord.

The Babylonians will bring so many war horses that the dust they kick up will cover the city like a dark cloud. The rumble of rushing chariot wheels and charging cavalry will shake the cracked city walls as soldiers charge through the broken gates. Earthly grandeur cannot withstand the overwhelming force God sends against it.

War horses will stomp through the streets of Tyre as Babylonian soldiers slaughter its inhabitants. The great stone pillars honoring their pagan gods and civic glory will crash down to the earth. Trusting in idols and military might always leads to complete ruin.

Invading soldiers will loot Tyre's vast storehouses, break down its fine homes, and sweep its stones, timber, and dirt into the sea. This was fully carried out when later conquerors like Alexander the Great pushed the mainland ruins into the water to build a causeway out to the island fortress. God's prophetic warnings are proven true with incredible historical accuracy.

The Lord will put a permanent end to the noisy music and merry songs that filled the markets and homes of Tyre. The sound of harps and celebration will be replaced by dead silence. Earthly partying and worldly joy quickly vanish when God's hand of discipline falls.

God will turn Tyre into a bare, flat rock where fishermen spread out their nets, and the city will never regain its former royal glory. The Lord has declared this sentence, and His spoken word will not fail. We can place our trust in God because what He promises will always come to pass.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critical scholars argue that this prophecy did not come true in every detail because an island city named Tyre was rebuilt and inhabited for centuries afterward.

notes.meaning: The Lord tells Tyre that all the surrounding islands and coastlands will shake with fear when they hear about her collapse. When neighboring nations hear the groaning of the wounded and the reports of slaughter, they will realize how vulnerable they are. Watching others fall should lead us to seek God's mercy rather than trusting in our own strength.

The rulers and wealthy merchant princes of the surrounding seaports will step down from their seats and remove their fine embroidered garments. In deep sorrow and fear, they will sit on the ground, trembling as they see how quickly Tyre was brought low. Worldly power and high status mean nothing when the Lord brings His judgment.

The mourning leaders will sing a funeral song of grief over the famous seaport that once ruled the Mediterranean. They will remember how Tyre used its naval fleet to terrify nearby nations and maintain iron control over sea trade. No nation can stay supreme forever by ruling through fear and greed.

Distant islands and coastal colonies will shudder in panic on the day of Tyre's downfall. Her trading partners will be deeply troubled because their primary economic lifeline and protection have vanished. Placing our security in trade and wealth will leave us helpless in times of disaster.

The Lord compares the ruin of Tyre to a deserted city swamped by deep, rushing ocean waters. This image pictures both the literal waves breaking over her crumbled harbor and the flood of foreign armies sent to overwhelm her. God rules over both the wild seas and the armies of the earth to accomplish His will.

God will send Tyre down into the Pit, the silent realm of the dead, to dwell among the ruined peoples of long ago. While Tyre remains desolate and forgotten in the grave, God will establish true life and glory among His people in their homeland. Worldly pride ends in darkness, but God preserves honor and hope for those who belong to Him.

The Lord will turn Tyre into a terrifying example of total ruin, and her glory will exist no more. Though travelers and merchants search for the ancient queen of the seas, they will never find her again. All worldly empires eventually pass away, but the kingdom of God remains forever.
